content.subject: Network Theory
content.hook: Can you zero out dependent sources when finding Thevenin resistance?
content.question: When finding Thevenin resistance in a linear circuit containing both independent and dependent sources, how are the sources treated?
options: Deactivate both independent and dependent sources
Keep all sources active and divide open-circuit voltage by short-circuit current
Deactivate only independent sources and apply an external test source
Deactivate only dependent sources and combine resistances directly
content.answerLine: Deactivate only independent sources and apply an external test source.
explanation: Independent sources are deactivated by replacing voltage sources with short circuits and current sources with open circuits.
Dependent sources cannot be turned off because their values depend on controlling variables within the active network.
Turning off a dependent source destroys the physical constraint it imposes on the other branch currents and voltages.
Instead, deactivate all independent sources and attach an external test source across the designated load terminals.
content.funFact: If a circuit contains only dependent sources and resistors, its open-circuit Thevenin voltage is identically zero!
content.outro: Watch out for dependent sources on your next exam and follow for more electrical engineering prep!

script.narration: Independent sources are deactivated by replacing voltage sources with short circuits and current sources with open circuits.
Dependent sources cannot be turned off because their values depend on controlling variables within the active network.
Turning off a dependent source destroys the physical constraint it imposes on the other branch currents and voltages.
Instead, deactivate all independent sources and attach an external test source across the designated load terminals.
This external excitation can be a test voltage of one volt or a test current of one ampere.
Measure the resulting current entering the terminal or the voltage developed across the applied test source.
The Thevenin resistance equals the test voltage divided by the test current at those terminals.
Alternatively, find the open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current, provided the open-circuit voltage is not zero.
Remember that setting dependent sources to zero is a fatal mistake in state competitive engineering examinations.
